top.name: Spider-speak
entries: Shulgurk can speak with spiders, with the same effects and limitations as speak with animals.

bot.name: Anadi Venom
entries:
Saving Throw DC 17 Fortitude
Maximum Duration 4 rounds
Stage 1 1d6 poison damage and off-guard (1 round)
Stage 2 1d6 poison damage, off-guard, and clumsy 1 (1 round)

bot.name: Attach Sanguine Hose
entries:
Shulgurk attempts to embed a toothy sphincter at the end of a leather hose attached to his infernal machine in the flesh of a living creature that's also within 10 feet of the infernal machine. The torturer makes an infernal machine hose Strike against the restrained creature, with a hit successfully attaching the hose to the creature, that's thereafter off-guard and susceptible to Exsanguinate Subject until the hose is detached. Safely removing an attached sanguine hose from a living subject requires spending an action to attempt a DC 16 Crafting or Medicine check, or a DC 20 Athletics check (these DCs increase by 4 if the Strike to attach the hose was a critical hit), with the following results.
Critical Success The hose detaches without additional damage to the subject.
Success The hose detaches from the subject fairly cleanly, but the toothy sphincter at its end manages to take a chunk of flesh as a souvenir, dealing 1d4 piercing damage to the subject.
Failure The hose separates from the skin with a sickening “plop” and a spurt of fresh blood. The subject takes 1d4 piercing damage and 1d6 persistent bleed damage
Critical Failure As failure, but the subject also becomes drained 1.

bot.name: Change Shape
entries: Shulgurk changes into his hybrid form, spider form, or human form. The above statistics assume he's in his hybrid form. While in human form, he can't use his fangs attack and loses his climb speed. While in spider form, he can't use weapons.

bot.name: Exsanguinate Subject
entries:
Frequency once per round
Effect Shulgurk manipulates the infernal machine to deal 1d6 persistent bleed damage as long as a creature remains attached to the infernal machine by a sanguine hose. If a creature takes this bleed damage, it must succeed at a DC 17 Fortitude save or become enfeebled 1 for 1 minute.

bot.name: Fire Cone
entries:
Frequency once per round
Effect Shulgurk releases a lever on the infernal machine to send a dose of lesser alchemist's fire through a pliable metal hose, dealing 1d8 fire damage in a 20-foot cone (DC 16 basic Reflex save). Each time Shulgurk uses this ability, reduce the total doses of lesser alchemist's fire available to the infernal machine by 1.

bot.name: Spin Silk
entries: By spending several minutes, Shulgurk can produce silk to craft items made of webbing or cloth. He can produce enough silk in a day to craft a single garment.

mid.name: Proof of Undeath
entries: A sanctum knight believes themself to be a living immortal, but if offered proof that they are in fact undead, they must succeed at a DC 20 Will save or become frightened 1 (or frightened 3 on a critical failure). On a critical success, they're temporarily immune to this fear for 24 hours. Once they recover from being frightened, their memories of the proof offered fade and they once again regard themselves as living immortals. Proof of undeath includes whenever they take vitality damage, whenever they restore HP as a result of void damage, or whenever a character within 30 feet presents evidence or an argument as a 2-action activity with the linguistic trait and succeeds at a DC 17 Deception, Diplomacy, or Intimidation check.

bot.name: Aeon Blast
entries:
The sanctum knight chooses one of the aeon stars, then fires it from its orbit to detonate into a 20-foot-radius blast at any point within 120 feet, dealing 2d6 damage to creatures in the area (basic DC 21 Reflex save). The damage type depends on the color of the aeon star.
Black Aeon Star void damage
Gold Aeon Star electricity damage
Green Aeon Star acid damage
White Aeon Star spirit damage

bot.name: Aeon Stars
entries: A sanctum knight has four tiny motes of light that constantly orbit their head. These four aeon stars are black, gold, green, and white, and each provides illumination equivalent to that of a lit candle. A sanctum knight can expend an aeon star to make an Aeon Blast, but once a sanctum knight has used all of their aeon stars, they become slowed 1. An expended aeon star returns to its orbit around the sanctum knight's head automatically after 1 hour has passed.

bot.name: Muddle Mind
entries: The first time each round a creature takes damage from a throneglass weapon wielded by a sanctum knight, it must attempt a DC 21 Will save to avoid becoming stupefied 1 for 1 minute (or stupefied 1 for 24 hours on a critical failure). Regardless of the result of its save, the creature is temporarily immune to muddle mind for 1 round.

mid.name: Nauseating Glyphs
mid.trigger: Lord Pandelay is hit by a weapon Strike
entries: Effect The runes on Lord Pandelay’s ebon regalia flash in an unpleasant shimmering blast of light, increasing Pandelay’s AC against the strike by 2 to AC 26, potentially causing the strike to miss or not be a critical hit. Pandelay reflexively directs this light to focus on any adjacent creature; that creature must succeed at a DC 21 Will save or become sickened 1 from the blast of color (sickened 2 on a critical failure). If there are no viable targets to direct this flash of light onto in an adjacent space (such as if Pandelay uses this reaction against a creature who uses a weapon with reach or a ranged weapon), then the nauseating glyphs affect Pandelay himself, and he must attempt the DC 21 Will save.

bot.name: Activate Glyph
entries: Lord Pandelay focuses his concentration on Twinslayer, causing one of the glyphs on the blade to glow and granting the sword one of three different effects, chosen from below.

bot.name: Enervating Glyph
entries: Twinslayer shimmers with seething black energy, and then Pandelay fires a beam of darkness from the blade, targeting a creature within 30 feet and dealing 4d6 void damage (DC 24 basic Fortitude save)

bot.name: Pallid Glyph
entries:
Twinslayer glows with a pale white sheen that inflicts overwhelming pain. This activation lasts for 1 minute or until Pandelay Activates Glyph again. When a creature takes damage from a Strike from Twinslayer, they must attempt a DC 24 Fortitude save with the following effects.
Critical Success The creature is unaffected and is temporarily immune to the pallid glyph for 24 hours.
Success The creature is unaffected.
Failure The creature becomes off-guard from the pain until the end of Pandelay’s next turn.
Critical Failure As failure, but the creature also falls prone from the pain.

bot.name: Twinstriking Glyph
entries: Twinslayer glows with coruscating red light for 1 minute or until Pandelay Activates Glyph again. During this time, a creature that takes damage from a strike from Twinslayer becomes marked, the wound glowing with flickering red radiance until the end of Pandelay’s turn. If Pandelay damages a different creature with a Strike from Twinslayer while a previous victim has been marked earlier that same round, the new creature struck becomes marked, and the previous target loses the mark. If that target is within 30 feet of Pandelay when it loses their mark, they take 1d6 persistent bleed damage as blood pours from the previously marked wound.

top.name: Site Bound
entries: Deravon’s ghost can travel anywhere in the Sanctum of Aroden (areas B29–B34) but not beyond.

mid.name: Helm Dependent
entries: Deravon is incorporeal, but the magical helm he wears is physical, perched atop his head as securely as if he were a physical creature. He cannot pass through solid objects while wearing his helm, but without it he is weakened. A PC can remove his helm with a DC 27 Athletics check to Disarm, and if Deravon's ghost critically fails a Reflex save, he must immediately attempt a second Reflex save against the same DC. On a failure, his helm topples from his head. While he can move through solid objects while his helm is off, he can't use Aeon Stars or Bow Before Me, and is slowed 1 as long as he remains without his helm.

mid.name: Rejuvenation
entries: Destroying Deravon's link to the world— his magical helm—prevents him from rejuvenating and allows him to move on to the afterlife once he is destroyed.

bot.name: Aeon Star’s Curse
entries:
Deravon’s ghost has four tiny motes of darkness that constantly orbit the glowing helm atop his head. When he activates the Aeon Star’s Curse, one of these motes of darkness fires from its orbit to strike a living creature within 120 feet. That creature takes 5d6 spirit damage and must attempt a DC 28 Will save. An expended Aeon Star returns to its orbit around Deravon’s head automatically after 1 hour has passed, but if no Aeon Stars orbit his head, Deravon’s ghost can’t activate Aeon Star’s Curse, and the Athletics check to Disarm his helm drops to DC 23.
Critical Success The creature is unaffected.
Success The creature takes 2d6 spirit damage.
Failure The creature takes 4d6 spirit damage and becomes stupefied 1 with an unlimited duration.
Critical Failure The creature takes 8d6 spirit damage and becomes stupefied 2 with an unlimited duration. In addition, they suffer from an overwhelming conviction that, at any moment, the Aeon Star might appear in the sky above, portending the end of all things. As long as they remain outdoors during the day or indoors or underground at any time of day, the cursed character is off-guard from this constant distraction. While outdoors at night, the cursed character is also slowed 1 from this spiritual conviction.

bot.name: Bow Before Me
entries:
Frequency once per round
Effect Deravon’s ghost can use the “Bow Before Aroden” activation of his helm at will as a single action once per round rather than once per day as a two-action activity, as long as the command he issues is to bow before him and not before Aroden.

bot.name: Slice of Death
entries:
Deravon’s ghost swings his ghostly longsword in an arc before him, unleashing a 30-foot cone of void energy. Creatures in the area take 8d6 void damage and must make a DC 28 Fortitude save against the following additional effects. Deravon’s ghost can’t use Slice Of Death for 1d4 rounds.
Critical Success The creature takes no damage and is unaffected.
Success The creature takes half damage.
Failure The creature takes full damage and an additional 2d6 persistent void damage as their flesh begins to rot away.
Critical Failure The creature takes double damage, 2d6 persistent void damage, and becomes slowed 1 as long as they continue taking the persistent void damage as their body begins to stiffen up as if from rigor mortis.

creature.name: Cherub

bot.name: Cherub’s Arrow
entries: The cherub concentrates on an arrow they have nocked in their bow, imbuing it with supernatural power before firing it at a target within 30 feet. The arrow inflicts no damage on a hit, and instead has one of the following effects, chosen by the cherub. While the cherub can use this ability every round if they so choose, they can never pick the same effect twice in a row. A creature struck must succeed at a DC 16 Will save or be affected as follows, depending on the cherub’s choice (on a critical hit, the creature takes a –2 penalty to the saving throw).

bot.name: Delight
entries: The target becomes off-guard as they become distracted by all the wonders of life until the start of the cherub’s next turn.

bot.name: Love
entries: The target becomes fascinated for 1 minute by a second, non-cherub creature within 30 feet of the cherub whom the target can see. This effect has the visual trait.

bot.name: Peace
entries: The target is filled with a sense of tranquility and takes a –1 status penalty to attack rolls for 1 minute.

bot.name: Regret
entries: The target becomes filled with shame and remorse, becoming sickened 1 (sickened 2 on a critical failure).

creature.flavor:
Subjects of stone fountain sculptures and religious paintings throughout the Universe, cherubs are minor celestials who seek to promote cooperation, peace, and above all else, love between mortal creatures. To many cherubs, the goal of nurturing love and affection between two diametrically opposed enemies is the height of bliss. While they have magical abilities and innate spells that can help them in these pursuits, most cherubs consider such methods as tactics of last resort, or tools to be reached for when passion turns to wrath and violence breaks out. Despite their belief in love conquering all, cherubs aren’t naive and understand that in some cases, love simply can’t bloom. Faced with such a quandary, the cherub instead seeks to minimize conflict, hoping to lay foundations that at some point in the future can lead to a peaceful or, even better, romantic resolution.

While cherubs are kindly, compassionate, and at worst maybe a little mischievous, certain fiends find them to be particularly annoying. These unholy agents of corruption take great pleasure in capturing cherubs and forcing them to act in ways against their very nature, in using magic to disguise themselves as cherubs in order to work their evil deeds while eroding a society’s trust in cherubic goodness, or simply relying on particularly realistic illusions to do the same. Using illusory creature to create a sinister cherub is a tactic many fiends are quite fond of.

Cherubs Of Many Planes

Cherubs can hail from any of the celestial Outer Planes—Elysium, Nirvana, and especially Heaven. Regardless of their origins, their goals remain the same: to seek out mortals and to encourage positive relationships between them, to spread kindness and love, and perhaps have a little good-hearted mischief along the way. The typical cherub presented here is one from Heaven—a pudgy, winged child. Those from Nirvana look more like small anthropomorphic animals, while those from Elysium are more slender and lithe, looking more like a bird-winged pixie.

creature.name: Heart Of Sarnax

top.name: Hear Heartbeat
entries: The Heart of Sarnax can hear a living creature’s heartbeat as a precise sense in the listed range.

bot.name: Speak to Inner Evils
entries:
Frequency once per round
Effect The Heart of Sarnax speaks to a creature it can hear the heartbeat of within 60 feet, beckoning that creature to give in to their inner desires to commit evil acts. The Heart of Sarnax attempts an Intimidation check against the target’s Will DC, with the following results.
Critical Success The inner evils take over fully, and the target becomes confused for 1 minute. While confused, the creature will never attack the Heart of Sarnax, attacking themself instead if the Heart of Sarnax is the only viable target. The Heart of Sarnax becomes quickened for 1 round, and can use the extra action only to Speak to Inner Evils.
Success The inner evils take over only briefly. The creature becomes confused for 1 round.
Failure The inner evils fail to take over fully but are still distracting. The creature becomes off-guard until the end of their next turn.
Critical Failure The creature resists their inner evils and is immune to Speak to Inner Evils from this point on. The Heart of Sarnax recoils in shock, taking 4d6 mental damage (DC 25 basic Will save).

bot.name: Void Beam
entries: The Heart of Sarnax fires a 60-foot line of spiraling, shadowy void energy from the cavity in its chest. Creatures in the area take 7d6 void damage (DC 24 basic Fortitude). The Heart of Sarnax can’t use Void Beam again for 1d4 rounds.

creature.flavor:
When Sarnax sought to purge his soul of all evils, the result was a physical manifestation of crystal that approximated the size and shape of his heart. The evil contained within remained quiescent as long as Sarnax lived, but upon his death, the item gained power, no longer held in check by Sarnax’s living soul. If returned to any version of the living Sarnax, this grown evil manifests into a creature made of solid ruby whose first and primary goal is the destruction of its source. Afterward, the Heart of Sarnax can turn its attention to the world, eager to visit upon reality all the evils, both petty and potent, that Sarnax might have pursued had he fallen from grace while alive.

Other Hearts

The Heart of Sarnax is a unique creature tied to an artifact of the same name that manifests in this construct form only in a specific situation (see the first interlude in Chapter 3 of this adventure), but creatures similar to the Heart of Sarnax could exist in your campaign if you wish. In this case, you should rename the construct into something less specific, such as Ruby Guardian or Ruby Warrior.

creature.name: Sanctum Knight

mid.name: Proof of Undeath
entries: A sanctum knight believes themself to be a living immortal, but if offered proof that they are in fact undead, they must succeed at a DC 20 Will save or become frightened 1 (or frightened 3 on a critical failure). On a critical success, they’re temporarily immune to this fear for 24 hours. Once they recover from being frightened, their memories of the proof offered fade and they once again regard themselves as living immortals. Proof of undeath includes whenever they take vitality damage, whenever they restore HP as a result of void damage, or whenever a character within 30 feet presents evidence or an argument as a 2-action activity with the linguistic trait and succeeds at a DC 17 Deception, Diplomacy, or Intimidation check.

bot.name: Aeon Blast
entries:
The sanctum knight chooses one of the aeon stars, then fires it from its orbit to detonate into a 20-foot-radius blast at any point within 120 feet, dealing 2d6 damage to creatures in the area (basic DC 18 Reflex save). The damage type depends on the color of the aeon star.
Black Aeon Star void damage
Gold Aeon Star electricity damage
Green Aeon Star acid damage
White Aeon Star spirit damage

bot.name: Aeon Stars
entries: A sanctum knight has four tiny motes of light that constantly orbit their head. These four aeon stars are black, gold, green, and white, and each provides illumination equivalent to that of a lit candle. A sanctum knight can expend an aeon star to make an Aeon Blast (see above), but once a sanctum knight has used all of their aeon stars, they become slowed 1. An expended aeon star returns to its orbit around the sanctum knight's head automatically after 1 hour has passed.

bot.name: Muddle Mind
entries: The first time each round a creature takes damage from a throneglass weapon wielded by a sanctum knight, it must attempt a DC 18 Will save to avoid becoming stupefied 1 for 1 minute (or stupefied 1 for 24 hours on a critical failure). Regardless of the result of its save, the creature is temporarily immune to muddle mind for 1 round.

creature.flavor:
The devoted Knights of the Aeon Star who chose to serve in the Sanctum of Aroden believed their tours of duty would last, at most, a few years, and that they would emerge from the sanctum with glory and prestige. In truth, when Aroden died, these knights slowly starved to death after becoming trapped within the Sanctum, only to rise from death when the malevolent forces from the Heart of Sarnax got into their bodies and drew back their souls to serve as sanctum knights. These rare undead are found only in the Sanctum of Aroden.

Life Eternal

While all sanctum knights are undead, they do not regard themselves as undead and instead believe they continue to live their previous lives as servants of Aroden who have been rewarded with immortality by him in return for their pledge of service.

creature.name: Weary

bot.name: Corpse
entries: Until the next time they act, the weary appears to be an unanimated corpse. They have an automatic result of 22 on Deception checks and DCs to pass as a corpse.

bot.name: Empty Yawn
entries:
Frequency once per hour
Effect The weary’s jaws stretch open to an unnatural extent, giving cry to a horrific, chilling wail of exhaustion that cuts into the minds of nearby living creatures. Instilled in their thoughts is the sensation of the anguish of being dead, yet conscious of the body’s slow decay. Living creatures within a 20-foot emanation take 1d6 mental damage with a DC 16 Will save.
Critical Success The creature is unaffected.
Success The creature takes half damage.
Failure The creature takes full damage and is frightened 1.
Critical Failure The creature takes double damage and is frightened 2.

bot.name: Exhausting Torpor
entries: When a living creature is bitten by a weary, the undead infects the living flesh with the exhaustion of the grave. The creature bitten must attempt a DC 16 Fortitude save or become enfeebled 1 for 1 round (enfeebled 2 for 1 round on a critical failure).

bot.name: Overwhelming Numbers
entries: A weary gains a +2 circumstance bonus on melee attack rolls against a target who has been struck earlier in that round by a different weary.

creature.flavor:
While the method of creating the weary is a well-kept secret of hryngar worshippers of Droskar, there’s nothing preventing other unholy spellcasters from transforming those who have worked themselves into an early grave into these pitiful, unsettling monsters. The weary don’t understand that they’ve died, only that they’re overwhelmed with a deep, aching exhaustion that fills them with a wretched hatred. Content to lie in a slowly rotting heap until they sense the approach of living creatures, when the weary lurch into activity it is with cries of pain and hopelessness. These undead creatures appear as rotting corpses who creep and crawl about on all fours, bodies too worn out to properly hold themselves fully upright.

Unlike zombies, which the weary are sometimes mistaken for, these undead retain their minds and memories of the final several agonizing weeks that led up to their deaths. They can rarely remember farther back than these final weeks and almost never remember their own names. While they’re capable of communication, they typically have nothing more to say then to moan and agonize over their pain, and to beg those they attack to end their suffering even as they do their best to chew and gnaw at the living meat that vexes them so.

The Broken Weary

The weary don’t last forever once created, and over time their exhaustion causes them to crumble into an unsettling mass of partially connected bodies, heads, and limbs that continue to twitch and moan but pose no significant threat. Sometimes, when enough of the broken weary compact upon each other in this way, they cease being creatures entirely and give rise to a single haunt.

creature.flavor:
The strapping apprentice armorer Blostin has arms like tree trunks, an indomitable heart, and a strong will to survive. He keeps a good nature even under extremely dire circumstances, taking the party's attempt to escape the Clan Orthux compound as an opportunity to prove to himself that he is just as brave and capable as he has always imagined himself to be. The Taldan man stands well over 6 feet tall, striking an imposing figure undercut slightly by his long, unkempt brown bangs, which cast a shadow on his eyes and make him look even younger than his 20 years. He wears the brown pocketed apron of his craft, just as he did the day he was abducted by unknown parties on the streets of the Ivy District. When the adventure begins, Blostin is more or less free of toiler's gruel poisoning.

Blostin was raised as an orphan in an Absalom slum by well-meaning missionaries and pastors before tending the water buckets at Embrey's Armory, the workshop of master armorer and weapon crafter Engleton Embrey, one of the most celebrated artisans in all of Absalom. The dwarf took an instant liking to the young boy, and when Blostin turned 12, Embrey welcomed him as a full apprentice. Now, 8 years later, old Embrey is looking to retire sometime soon, and Blostin knows he has a good chance to inherit some or all of the business—only he doesn't really want to be an artisan. Especially since meeting the PCs and trying to escape the hryngar compound, Blostin is now more sure than ever that if he makes it out of here alive, destiny has something more in store for him than hammering out swords and shields for gladiators and adventuring heroes. Still, Engleton Embrey has been like a father to him, and he's not at all sure how he plans to break the news to the old dwarf or how his mentor will handle his disappointment.

Blostin comes alive in battle, yelling out what he thinks is witty banter, congratulating allies on excellent blows, shouting warnings to “watch out!” (whether helpful or not), and so on. As the adventure continues and shifts from the Orthux compound to the Sanctum of Aroden, Blostin loses a great deal of his bravado, especially if any of the PCs or other freed captive NPCs are killed. Revenge against hryngars he understands, but ancient curses, undead sanctum knights, and robbing the tomb of a church patriarch of Aroden deeply upset him and shake his confidence a bit. In the sanctum, Blostin starts to strongly consider the idea that he might not make it out alive and that all his daydreams of becoming an adventurer or a fighting hero on the field of the Irorium might have been for nothing.

creature.name: Elharris

mid.name: Scholarly Assistance
mid.trigger: An allied creature attempts a skill check to Recall Knowledge while not in combat
entries:
Requirements Elharris has recovered from her poisoning and is communicative
Effect Elharris provides additional context, theories, and suppositions to assist the triggering creature’s attempt to Recall Knowledge, granting them a +1 circumstance bonus to the check. If the triggering creature is attempting to Recall Knowledge from a subject that’s particularly academic or artistic in nature, this increases to a +2 circumstance bonus.

creature.flavor:
Elharris is a formerly serene artist and scholar from Kyonin visiting Absalom to study at the Arcanamirium. While returning alone from a quiet evening with friends at an Ivy District theater, she fell prey to a gang of human kidnappers in the employ of the crime boss Gewgaw. The mercurial tengu had decided to add an elf to his collection, and his agents selected Elharris at random. The abduction shocked Elharris, but it also confirmed every prejudice she had toward humans.

Elharris still wears the expensive gown she wore to the theater on her last night in Absalom, albeit with numerous tears and stains that somewhat lessen its original dramatic impact. She has violet eyes and an ugly bruise on the left side of her face, “encouragement” from the ogre Mullun to not cause trouble. When the adventure begins, Elharris is deeply in thrall to the mind-numbing toiler's gruel. Until she regains her senses, she is cowardly and unwilling to enter combat unless ordered to do so. As with the other captives, the effects of the poison wane as the adventure progresses, wearing off entirely after three days. Although Elharris is an apprentice wizard in addition to her artistic and scholarly accomplishments, the impact of the poison on her spellcasting ability extends longer than her other symptoms. She won't regain her spellcasting ability until she fully recovers for some time in Absalom after the conclusion of this adventure.

Elharris's mind remains clouded for much of her time in the Orthux compound, but by the time the party finds itself in the bas-relief galleries in Sarnax's tomb, her lifelong interest in art and history finally begins to override the numbing effects of the poison, and she starts to emerge from her shell. If she has writing supplies (such as might be recovered in area A18), Elharris sketches the figures of Sarnax she sees in the gallery and transcribes their associated inscriptions. Her keen ability to interpret images and symbols—plus the voracious curiosity about legends and mythology critical to a complete understanding of art history— makes Elharris a good source of information about the art in the sanctum.

creature.name: Greely

bot.name: Additional Information
entries:
Requirements Greely isn’t in combat, and a PC has missed or forgotten a key piece of information
Effect Greely can step in to provide additional information or context, or remind the PCs of something they learned but appear to have forgotten, provided the information in question has something to do with history, Absalom’s society, or one of Greely’s Lore skills. Once he provides this aid, he grows smug and disdainful, and won’t provide Additional Information again for the remainder of the day unless, at your discretion, the PCs really need the extra hint.

creature.flavor:
The constantly sneering, never satisfied, cantankerous old curmudgeon Greely runs a posh antique shop called This & That on the eastern edge of Absalom's Foreign Quarter. He has a good eye for antiques and makes a tidy profit off his customers, whom he tends to gouge deeply on price. Greely is quite knowledgeable about the noble houses of Absalom, but his comprehension is soaked in cynicism, as are his comments regarding the topic.

The aged merchant is 73 years old and attributes his longevity so far to a healthy reliance on cowardice. He doesn't fight unless ordered to, preferring to keep several members of the party between himself and any perceived danger. He is methodical, cautious, and wants very much to escape his current predicament alive (and perhaps with an armful of valuable antiquities no one would ever miss).

A few months ago, Greely bragged of his shop's treasures to the wrong paid companion, and word of his collection reached Gewgaw. The first few missives from the tengu crime lord were polite, inquiring about specific items in the collection and asking about prices or openness to trades in kind. Greely rebuffed the inquiries. This led to harsher tactics from Gewgaw that eventually escalated to Greely's abduction from an Absalom street corner. He's worried that his entire shop has been emptied since he was kidnapped and seethes with anger that his downfall came at the hands of a collector who loves antiques even more than him.

Once free of toiler's gruel poisoning, Greely's mind is incredibly sharp, and he's the first to explain the burden of being more intelligent and wiser than just about everyone else. He constantly second guesses the PCs' ideas, demanding to know each step of their plans and occasionally attempting to outright veto elements that make him uncomfortable.

In the Orthux compound, Greely is too drugged up and cowardly to make much of an impression, but once the party gets down to the antiquities-packed Sanctum of Aroden, he becomes more engaged. He is a good source for additional information of a historical nature that the PCs might have overlooked unintentionally or by making poor dice rolls. Likewise, he is an excellent source of details on Absalom nobles, whom he generally despises. Greely is always ready to provide a lecture on virtually any subject. He bitterly scolds anyone who he feels isn't paying close-enough attention to his wisdom.

He is not exactly a delight to be around.

creature.name: Irabel Of Eiseth

bot.name: Asp Stance
entries: Irabel enters a stance wherein she adopts a fluid, sinuous set of motions that mimic the striking of a venomous serpent. Her fist Strikes deal piercing damage while she’s in Asp Stance, and she gains a +1 circumstance bonus to AC. When she targets the same creature with two Strikes from her Flurry of Blows, if both Strikes hit, the target becomes sickened 1 from the pain.

bot.name: Flurry of Blows
entries:
Frequency once per round
Effect Irabel makes two fist Strikes. If both hit the same creature, combine the damage for the purpose of resistances and weaknesses. Apply her multiple attack penalty to the Strikes normally.

bot.name: Powerful Fist
entries: Irabel doesn’t take the normal –2 circumstance penalty when making a lethal attack with her fist or any other unarmed attack.

creature.flavor:
Irabel was born in Absalom just over 20 years ago, the youngest daughter of Lady Xansippe, the city's high priestess of Cheliax, and Lord Gulv, an influential Chelaxian diplomat who now serves as that nation's official ambassador to Absalom. Although she is a noble in high standing with one of the city's most influential houses, Irabel had a difficult upbringing, and she shows few signs of having been raised in luxury. Her father abandoned the family to serve Queen Abrogail in the capital city of Egorian when Irabel was only 2, and for reasons Irabel never fully understood, her mother always seemed to hold her in contempt, focusing what little affection she was willing to share upon Irabel's older sisters, Azoria and Seichya. On Irabel's 10th birthday, Lord Gulv and all of his daughters survived an assassination attempt by an Andoren radical who hurled an alchemical bomb at their passing carriage. Expecting further attacks and eager to protect their family line should tragedy strike true on a second attempt, Lord Gulv and Lady Xansippe committed Irabel to a convent of the devil queen Eiseth in Westcrown, where the Sisterhood of the Golden Erinyes could protect her against the brutal politics of Cheliax and its enemies. There she has remained for the last decade in complete isolation from her family.

As part of her religious instruction, Irabel studied and practiced to become an assassin—an ironic focus given the reasons for her being sent to the convent in the first place. Yet further irony saw this training bringing her once more into the circle of her father and her family, the Tevineg clan. Central to the lore of the family—and, to be fair, its longevity and success—was an infernal pact signed by all members that dictated they were never to openly attack or try to slay any other member of the Tevineg clan. Following a recent return to Absalom to assume the duties as Cheliax's formal ambassador to the city, Lord Gulv sought to further consolidate his power within his own family. He had always resented the fact that he had married into the family and that his wife, Xansippe, thus outranked him as the house's official Scion Lord. Ever the tactician, Lord Gulv devised a way around the pact they all had signed and used his contact with the Sisterhood (unbeknownst to Irabel) to put his plan into motion.

Without making much attempt to cover his involvement, Lord Gulv hired the Sisterhood to assassinate the wife of Felden Remarios, an old political rival in Egorian. Gulv knew that Remarios would strike back in revenge by reciprocally assassinating his own “beloved” wife, Xansippe. Gulv would then become the supreme noble of the Tevineg family, allowing him to consolidate his power and finally bring his older daughters and other lesser members of the house and their allies fully into his sphere of influence. Gulv was right to anticipate his rival would use the same order of assassins to gain revenge, but he didn't count on the strength of the Sisterhood's whisper network. Although the Sisterhood tried to keep Irabel from discovering her father's tawdry business, word did reach her about the killer the leaders of the Sisterhood dispatched to fulfill Felden's contract on Xansippe. Irabel fled the convent that night, tracked down and murdered her sister-assassin, then decided to return to Absalom for a reckoning with her family.

For there was one other element of Gulv's master plan that the almighty Chimera had not accounted for—as part of her training and dedication to Eiseth, Irabel swore herself as a daughter of the Erinyes Queen, renouncing all ties to the family of her birth and releasing her from the bonds of the Tevineg pact by the laws of Hell. Although she harbors deep resentment toward her entire family, she decided before she even reached Absalom that her father had to die. After establishing herself in the city for a few weeks, during which she tracked the movements of her birth sisters, mother, and father, she finally decided to begin her confrontations with her oldest sister, Seichya, with whom she had always felt the closest bond. After more than a decade apart, however, Seichya thought of Irabel more as a stranger than a beloved sibling, and after a few tense moments the elder sister ordered her devil guards to capture Irabel and throw her into the Brine prison, loyally reporting Irabel's unexpected appearance to her father. Fearing complication at a critical juncture of his plan to prepare for the Test of the Starstone, Lord Gulv instructed Seichya to include Irabel in a group of prisoners he planned to send down to Clan Orthux by way of the Fall's End crime lord Gewgaw, hoping to treat Irabel to a final lesson in humility for daring to act against the family's best interests (naturally, Lord Gulv's hypocrisy is lost on him).

Stripped of the ceremonial habit of her order prior to being handed over to the Clan Orthux hryngars, Irabel is clothed in hand-me-down rags salvaged from the corpse of a captive who previously died of exhaustion. At the wrists, neckline, and ankles, the outfit fails to cover the edges of an elaborate full-body tattoo consisting of devilish symbols and Diabolic script, the mark of a Sister of the Golden Erinyes who has completed her training. Irabel is self-conscious about explaining her tattoos to strangers.

Irabel is slim and lithe like a gymnast. Even her casual movements seem deliberate, and in most cases, she conducts herself with the quiet grace one might expect from a nun. She is, however, quick to anger and prone to derision and sarcasm when aggrieved.

 As part of her religious instruction, Irabel studied and practiced to become an assassin—an ironic focus given the reasons for her being sent to the convent in the first place. Yet further irony saw this training bringing her once more into the circle of her father and her family, the Tevineg clan. Central to the lore of the family—and, to be fair, its longevity and success—was an infernal pact signed by all members that dictated they were never to openly attack or try to slay any other member of the Tevineg clan. Following a recent return to Absalom to assume the duties as Cheliax's formal ambassador to the city, Lord Gulv sought to further consolidate his power within his own family. He had always resented the fact that he had married into the family and that his wife, Xansippe, thus outranked him as the house's official Scion Lord. Ever the tactician, Lord Gulv devised a way around the pact they all had signed and used his contact with the Sisterhood (unbeknownst to Irabel) to put his plan into motion.

 Without making much attempt to cover his involvement, Lord Gulv hired the Sisterhood to assassinate the wife of Felden Remarios, an old political rival in Egorian. Gulv knew that Remarios would strike back in revenge by reciprocally assassinating his own “beloved” wife, Xansippe. Gulv would then become the supreme noble of the Tevineg family, allowing him to consolidate his power and finally bring his older daughters and other lesser members of the house and their allies fully into his sphere of influence. Gulv was right to anticipate his rival would use the same order of assassins to gain revenge, but he didn't count on the strength of the Sisterhood's whisper network. Although the Sisterhood tried to keep Irabel from discovering her father's tawdry business, word did reach her about the killer the leaders of the Sisterhood dispatched to fulfill Felden's contract on Xansippe. Irabel fled the convent that night, tracked down and murdered her sister-assassin, then decided to return to Absalom for a reckoning  with  her family.

 For there was one other element of Gulv's master plan that the almighty Chimera had not accounted for—as part of her training and dedication to Eiseth, Irabel swore herself as a daughter of the Erinyes Queen, renouncing all ties to the family of her birth and releasing her from the bonds of the Tevineg pact by the laws of Hell. Although she harbors deep resentment toward her entire family, she decided before she even reached Absalom that her father had to die. After establishing herself in the city for a few weeks, during which she tracked the movements of her birth sisters, mother, and father, she finally decided to begin her confrontations with her oldest sister, Seichya, with whom she had always felt the closest bond. After more than a decade apart, however, Seichya thought of Irabel more as a stranger than a beloved sibling, and after a few tense moments the elder sister ordered her devil guards to capture Irabel and throw her into the Brine prison, loyally reporting Irabel's unexpected appearance to her father. Fearing complication at a critical juncture of his plan to prepare for the Test of the Starstone, Lord Gulv instructed Seichya to include Irabel in a group of prisoners he planned to send down to Clan Orthux by way of the Fall's End crime lord Gewgaw, hoping to treat Irabel to a final lesson in humility for daring to act against the family's best interests (naturally, Lord Gulv's hypocrisy is lost on him).

 Stripped of the ceremonial habit of her order prior to being handed over to the Clan Orthux hryngars, Irabel is clothed in hand-me-down rags salvaged from the corpse of a captive who previously died of exhaustion. At the wrists, neckline, and ankles, the outfit fails to cover the edges of an elaborate full-body tattoo consisting of devilish symbols and Diabolic script, the mark of a Sister of the Golden Erinyes who has completed her training. Irabel is self-conscious about explaining her tattoos to strangers.

 Irabel is slim and lithe like a gymnast. Even her casual movements seem deliberate, and in most cases, she conducts herself with the quiet grace one might expect from a nun. She is, however, quick to anger and prone to derision and sarcasm when aggrieved.

bot.name: Martial Performance
entries: When Jona has a courageous anthem, rallying anthem, or song of strength composition active, and he damages an enemy with a Strike, the spell's duration is extended by 1 round.

bot.name: Signature Spells

creature.flavor:
Thirty years ago, Jona Clay was a popular up-and- coming Pathfinder Society field agent with several exploits published in the Pathfinder Chronicles and a bright political future ahead of him in the leadership of the Grand Lodge of Absalom. Then, one day, he simply disappeared. Most of his colleagues assumed he had been killed in one of the siege castles littering the Cairnlands of Absalom's outskirts. Rumors among some of his friends and junior agents he'd brought into the organization told of a mission gone wrong in the Mwangi Expanse—or maybe it was Osirion—and a curse that kept him isolated from his former colleagues for fear that the wasting contagion might spread. Those who knew him best wondered if he had simply lost interest and wandered away, never to return.

In truth, Jona's disappearance was mired in tragedy. On one of his many adventures in central Avistan, while visiting a rustic village of little historical import on the way to explore a promising Third Crusade tomb, Jona Clay encountered a farm boy named Ellund, who dreamed of one day taking up a wayfinder and sword in service to the Pathfinder Society. Jona spent an afternoon encouraging the young man, even leaving behind a favorite old shortsword—the weapon he had held while daydreaming of adventures as a youth himself—with instructions that Ellund return it to him when he was ready to venture to the Grand Lodge in Absalom and join the ranks of the Society as a new recruit. A mere two days after leaving, Jona saw a column of thick black smoke rising on the horizon back in the direction of Ellund's farm. He immediately abandoned his original mission and sped back to the settlement only to discover smoldering ruins and fresh corpses—Ellund and his whole family had been murdered by bandits. Worse, Jona's old shortsword lay broken at the young man's side. Relying on Jona's lessons of bravery and swordplay, Ellund had tried his best to protect his family just as a Pathfinder would— but the boy and his family still died.

Despondent and overwhelmed with a sense of responsibility for Ellund's grim fate, Jona was haunted by nightmares for months, plagued by terrible dreams of drowning in a lake of blood, pulled down by dozens of hands. He quit his quarters at the Grand Lodge, leaving behind only his abandoned longsword and a blade fragment of the broken shortsword that had sealed Ellund's fate. No one in Absalom ever saw Jona Clay again.

But Jona Clay did not abandon Absalom, and he did not abandon the Pathfinder Society. Instead, he donned a disguise and assumed a new identity as Joran Culddammas, member in good standing of the Union of Artisans. He bought a home in the Ivy District, where he married Larissa Lorn, a part-time singer and full- time upper functionary in the Guild of Actors and Performers. Then, he set up shop as a humble woodcarver, with a workshop overlooking one of the district's busiest markets. There he served as an informant and secret member of the Pathfinder Society, recruiting new members of the organization through his wife's contacts among the city's performing artists.

Over the years, the masked ruling body of the Pathfinder Society—the Decemvirate— called upon Jona's services more and more, promoting him to the rank of venture-captain, even as his status within the Society and true identity remained a closely guarded secret to all but a small cadre of agents. Recently, the Decemvirate ordered him to accompany Shevala Iorae down into the tunnels beneath Absalom's Puddles district in an attempt to locate the long-lost location of the Sanctum of Aroden. Jona stands just over 6 feet tall. He has a lean frame and an open, trusting face. His graying hair recedes at the temples, adding a hint of fine age and distinction to his naturally handsome features. He wears a filthy outfit like most of the other prisoners but soon supplements his kit with aeon armor taken from the sanctum knights. In combat, he uses his bardic abilities to aid allies, but otherwise hangs back and observes how the PCs handle themselves.

Jona particularly appreciates any PC who returns the Pathfinder Society signet ring he left in area A4 and his wayfinder from the Orthux overlord's treasure cache in area A18. He is kind and slow to anger, and he tends to gravitate toward younger or more impressionable members of the party, attempting to mentor them but also warning them of the dangers of the adventuring life and the great burden of responsibility that falls upon adventurers—and particularly members of the Pathfinder Society. Although he shares the same rank as Shevala, he defers to her more often than not, as her public persona as a popular leader in the Society and lack of high-profile, costly failures confirms that her skills as a venture-captain are superior to his own.

bot.name: Distracting Halfling
entries:
Requirements Krell has taken 2 actions
Effect Krell scuttles around underfoot and behind a foe to leave them open to an attack by an ally. He attempts to Tumble Through a single creature’s space. If he’s successful, that creature is off-guard to the next attack made against them before Krell’s next turn.

bot.name: Sneak Attack
entries: Krell does an additional 1d6 precision damage to off-guard targets.

creature.flavor:
Krell grew up in Copperwood, just outside Absalom's northeast walls, a child of servants working in the Petal District. A year ago, Krell used his parents' keys to gain access to the manor home they serviced, attempting to steal several of the expensive art objects he'd heard his parents discussing. Unfortunately for Krell, the owners caught him in the act, and it took every ounce of loyalty his parents had earned to keep him out of jail. The scandal was severe enough that Krell's family disowned him and kicked him out of their home, cutting off contact with the son who had brought so much shame upon them.

Instead of taking this humiliation as a sign to live his life in a more wholesome direction, Krell decided to lean into his newfound independence from his family's rigid values and make the most of every opportunity for theft or burglary that happened to cross his path. He achieved moderate success in his favorite neighborhood, the Coins, where he eventually managed to afford a modest apartment of his own.

His crimes soon attracted the attention of the gang known as the Puddlejumpers led by the cruel halfling Benkt Slipshod. The Puddlejumpers warned Krell off their territory, unless of course he wanted to join up with them. When he refused on the grounds of their terrible reputation and cruelty, Slipshod knocked him out, tied him up, and traded him to Gewgaw for a pair of copper necklaces strewn with silver plates adorned with minor gemstones.

When encountered as a prisoner of Clan Orthux, Krell wears a soiled tan leather jerkin over a torn dark blue shirt and breeches with holes in the knees. He has curly red hair and bushy sideburns. His expression is warm, his eyes curious. He loudly professes that his primary interest is getting home to his apartment in the Coins, but he's easily distracted by opportunities to increase his personal wealth and isn't above encouraging the PCs to further investigate places like the Tomb of Sarnax or the Ship Chamber in search of plunder. An incorrigible thief, Krell can't resist looking for loot, even as he claims to be solely focused on escape.

At the beginning of the adventure, Krell is the least affected by toiler's gruel of all the members of his prison cell. He feels no special compulsion to follow orders and is fiercely protective of his fellow prisoners, pushing back strongly if the PCs attempt to abuse the other captives or callously order them into great danger simply for the convenience. He teams up with the similarly level-headed Blostin to make sure that his fellow captives are protected.

creature.name: Labella
creature.flavor:
Labella was born and raised in Absalom's Ivy District, the only child in a fourth generation of actors, performers, and dancers who have always called the city's arts district their home. She is a member in good standing with the Street Performers and Actor's Guild, and until recently was a rising star of Absalom's theater scene thanks to her eye-turning living tableaux performances at the Grand Dance Hall of Kortos in the Coins District. Labella owes her imprisonment by the hryngars to just such a performance, wherein an attempt to curry favor with Dance Hall patron, Lady Gloriana Morilla, by aggrandizing her home nation of Taldor with a vicious criticism of Cheliax stirred the annoyance of Lady Xansippe of House Tevineg, who also happened to be in attendance at the event and ended up leaving early after Labella's scandalous showing. Xansippe complained to her eldest daughter, Seichya, who had Labella kidnapped and interred at the Brine Prison, where Seichya serves as warden. From there, the dancer was swiftly “disappeared” into the custody of the Fall's End crime boss Gewgaw, from whence she was dispatched to the Clan Orthux compound as a prisoner.

When first encountered by the PCs, Labella is deeply in thrall to toiler's gruel. Prince Thorgrim is the youngest of four sons of King Borogrim the Hale, regent of the dwarf kingdoms of the Five Kings Mountains. With little prospect of inheriting his father's throne, Thorgrim took up life as a champion of Torag, venturing throughout the Lake Encarthan region as a sort of unofficial ambassador of the dwarves to the varied peoples living in the area. The longer Thorgrim spent away from his father's court and the company of other dwarves, the more he found himself succumbing to vices, and it wasn't long before Thorgrim started picking up nicknames like “the Partying Prince.” Reports of scandals related to his lechery and drunkenness didn't take long to reach the ears of his weary father in Highhelm, and even before the final indignity that split him from his family, the disapproval of his fellow dwarves grew as the physical distance between them increased. Finally, in 4705 ar, Thorgrim's wild lifestyle saw him imprisoned in a small town in Nirmathas, where he was very nearly killed by a corrupt jailer who wished to extort his father for a literal king's ransom. When Borogrim refused the jailer's blackmail, and in fact disowned his son in the text of his reply, Thorgrim assumed all was lost, and that he would probably die in that jail.

And he would have, if not for a timely liberation at the hands of a coterie of zealots of the Living God Razmir, who came to spread the influence of their cult in Nirmathas and who knew that an influential noble like Thorgrim could help their cause. They rescued him and incorporated him into their retinue. It wasn't long before Thorgrim came to align himself with the cult of Razmir, lured by the sweet words of his rescuers.

For years, he operated all over the Lake Encarthan region. Though he has visited Razmir many times and knows the Living God personally, he never mentions having been there. Recently, Razmir (in the disguise of Lord Synarr Daidalos, a recent arrival in Absalom) ordered Thorgrim to attend to him in the City at the Center of the World, to serve as his personal agent and operative there. Razmir somehow got word of the Chimera's interest in the Dead God's Hand, and since the Living God also intends to take the Test of the Starstone, he dispatched Prince Thorgrim into the sewers to snatch the hand before the Chimera could.

Thorgrim is evil but friendly in a boisterous, back-slapping way that masks his villainy and makes him fun to be around. He likes calling himself “Prince” Thorgrim, but he doesn't appreciate questions into this aspect of his past.
